blocks.text: Duplicate rows are one of the quietest ways a dataset lies to you. Nothing looks wrong when you print df.head(), nothing throws an error, and a model will happily train on the data anyway. But if the same customer, the same transaction, or the same sensor reading shows up in your table twice, every statistic computed from that column is now subtly wrong, and a model can become overconfident about a pattern it did not actually see twice in the real world, only twice in your spreadsheet.
This lesson covers how to find duplicate records, how to decide which copies to keep, and why removing them is not always the automatic right answer it first appears to be.
1. What Counts As A Duplicate
The word duplicate hides two very different problems underneath it. One is mechanical and easy to catch. The other requires judgment and is genuinely hard.
1.1 Exact Duplicates

An exact duplicate is a row where every single column matches another row exactly, same value, same type, same everything. If you laid the two rows side by side, you could not tell them apart. This is the easy case, because a computer can check it mechanically with a straightforward comparison, no interpretation required.
1.2 Near Duplicates (Fuzzy Duplicates)

A near duplicate, sometimes called a fuzzy duplicate, is a row that clearly represents the same real world entity as another row but does not match it character for character. The same customer entered twice with slightly different spelling, an extra trailing space in a name field, 'Jon Smith' next to 'John Smith', or an email address typed once in lowercase and once with a stray capital letter. A computer cannot flag these with a simple equality check, because technically the values are different. Catching these requires more judgment, and often more tooling, than exact duplicates do.

blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
blocks.content: Exact duplicates have one correct mechanical answer: they are copies, remove the extras. Near duplicates do not have one correct mechanical answer, two rows that look similar might genuinely be the same entity, or might genuinely be two different people who happen to share a common name. Treat the two problems separately.

blocks.text: 2. How Duplicates Typically Enter A Dataset

Duplicates rarely appear because someone typed the same row in twice on purpose. They tend to come from a handful of predictable sources, and knowing the source often tells you which kind of duplicate you are dealing with.

items: Double form submissions: a user clicks submit, the page is slow to respond, they click submit again, and now there are two identical (or nearly identical) records for the same signup or order.

Merging data from multiple sources that overlap: you combine an export from one system with an export from another, and some records genuinely exist in both because the two systems were never fully independent to begin with.
ETL bugs that reprocess the same batch twice: a pipeline fails partway through, gets rerun without clearing what it already wrote, and the same day's data lands in the table a second time.

blocks.text: Form resubmissions tend to produce exact duplicates, since the same input gets written the same way. Merges across systems tend to produce near duplicates, since each system may have its own formatting quirks for the same underlying entity.
3. Finding And Counting Exact Duplicates
pandas gives you duplicated() to flag exact duplicate rows as a boolean mask, the same shape as isna() from the missing values lesson, just checking a different condition.

code.content:
df.duplicated()
# 0    False
# 1    False
# 2     True   <- this row is identical to an earlier row
# 3    False
# dtype: bool

blocks.text: By default, duplicated() marks the first occurrence of a repeated row as False and every later occurrence as True, since the first one is treated as the original and anything after it is treated as the copy.
3.1 Counting How Many Duplicates You Have

Chaining .sum() onto duplicated() gives you a single number, exactly the same trick used for isna().sum() when counting missing values. This is usually one of the first checks worth running on a freshly loaded DataFrame.

That single number tells you how big the problem is before you decide how to handle it. A handful of duplicate rows out of a hundred thousand is a very different situation from a third of your dataset being duplicated, and the second case usually means something upstream is broken, not just a little sloppy.
4. Removing Exact Duplicates With drop_duplicates
drop_duplicates() removes the rows that duplicated() would flag as True, returning a new DataFrame with only the rows it decided to keep.
The real decision is not whether to call drop_duplicates, it is which copy to keep when a duplicate is found, and that is exactly what the keep parameter controls.
4.1 The keep Parameter, Precisely
keep decides which occurrence, among a group of duplicate rows, survives the drop.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Value","Behavior"],"rows":[["keep='first' (default)","Keeps the first occurrence of each duplicated row, drops every occurrence after it."],["keep='last'","Keeps the last occurrence of each duplicated row, drops every occurrence before it."],["keep=False","Drops ALL copies, including the first one. Nothing from that duplicate group survives."]]}

code.content:
df.drop_duplicates(keep='first')  # default, keeps the earliest row in each duplicate group
df.drop_duplicates(keep='last')   # keeps the most recent row in each duplicate group
df.drop_duplicates(keep=False)    # removes every row that had ANY duplicate, keeps none of them

blocks.text: keep='last' is genuinely useful when later rows in your DataFrame represent more recent, more corrected, or more complete versions of the same record, for example a log of profile updates where the newest row should win. keep=False is useful when a duplicate signals that a record is ambiguous or untrustworthy altogether, and you would rather discard it entirely than arbitrarily pick one of the copies to represent the truth.
5. Checking Duplicates On A Subset Of Columns
Both duplicated() and drop_duplicates() accept a subset parameter, which restricts the comparison to only the columns you name instead of requiring every single column in the row to match.

This matters because requiring a full row match is often too strict for the real question you are trying to answer. Two rows might represent the same customer, same email, same person, but differ slightly in a phone number field, a last login timestamp, or a notes column that gets updated independently. A full row comparison would say these are not duplicates at all, even though for the purpose of counting unique customers they clearly are. Passing subset=['email'] tells pandas to treat two rows as duplicates whenever they share an email, regardless of what else differs between them.

subset also accepts a list of several columns together, for cases where uniqueness is defined by a combination of fields rather than any single one, such as subset=['first_name', 'last_name', 'date_of_birth'] to catch the same person registered twice under two different customer IDs.
6. Worked Example: Before And After
Say you load a small orders table and it looks like this.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

data = {
    'order_id':   [101, 102, 102, 103, 104, 104],
    'customer':   ['Asha', 'Ravi', 'Ravi', 'Meera', 'Kiran', 'Kiran'],
    'item':       ['Pen', 'Notebook', 'Notebook', 'Bag', 'Bottle', 'Bottle'],
    'amount':     [10, 40, 40, 250, 90, 90],
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df.shape)
# (6, 4)

blocks.text: Rows 1 and 2 are identical (order_id 102 appears twice), and rows 4 and 5 are identical (order_id 104 appears twice). Checking with duplicated() confirms exactly that.

code.content:
print(df.duplicated().sum())
# 2

print(df[df.duplicated(keep=False)])
#    order_id customer      item  amount
# 1       102     Ravi  Notebook      40
# 2       102     Ravi  Notebook      40
# 4       104    Kiran    Bottle      90
# 5       104    Kiran    Bottle      90

blocks.text: Using keep=False here (only for inspection, not for the actual drop) shows both copies of every duplicated group, which is a handy way to eyeball what is about to be removed before you commit to removing it. Now drop them for real, keeping the first occurrence of each.

code.content:
df_clean = df.drop_duplicates(keep='first')
print(df_clean.shape)
# (4, 4)
print(df_clean)
#    order_id customer      item  amount
# 0       101     Asha       Pen      10
# 1       102     Ravi  Notebook      40
# 3       103    Meera       Bag     250
# 4       104    Kiran    Bottle      90

blocks.text: Six rows went in, four came out, and the row count dropping from 6 to 4 is the concrete signal that two exact duplicate order rows were removed.
7. Near Duplicate Detection

Exact matching only catches copies that are byte for byte identical. It will completely miss 'Ravi Kumar' next to 'ravi kumar ', or 'ravi.kumar@gmail.com' next to 'Ravi.Kumar@gmail.com'. Catching these starts with normalization.

Lowercasing, stripping whitespace, and collapsing repeated spaces before comparing turns a lot of what looks like a near duplicate into an exact duplicate in disguise. This alone catches a large share of real world cases, and it is a cheap step worth doing before reaching for anything fancier.

What normalization cannot fix is genuine spelling variation, 'Jon Smith' versus 'John Smith', or 'Rajesh Sharma' versus 'Rajesh Sharrma'. For that, string similarity techniques come in. A library like fuzzywuzzy or its faster successor rapidfuzz computes a similarity score between two strings, typically from 0 to 100, and you flag any pair scoring above some threshold as a candidate duplicate.

code.content:
from rapidfuzz import fuzz

score = fuzz.ratio('John Smith', 'Jon Smith')
print(score)
# 89, high similarity, worth a closer look

blocks.text: Notice the phrase candidate duplicate, not confirmed duplicate. This is a genuinely harder problem than exact matching, and it is rarely safe to automatically delete a row purely because a similarity score crossed some cutoff. The standard approach is to use the score to surface a shortlist of likely pairs and route that shortlist to a human reviewer, rather than letting the threshold silently delete data on its own. Automatic fuzzy deletion has a real failure mode: two genuinely different people who happen to share a very similar name can get merged into one, quietly erasing a real record.
8. When Removing Duplicates Is The Wrong Call

It is tempting to treat drop_duplicates as a safe default cleaning step to run on every dataset. It is not always safe, and the reason is that what counts as a duplicate depends on the domain, not just on the data.

Consider a transaction log. A customer who buys the exact same item twice in one day, same product, same price, same store, produces two rows that are identical in every column you might compare, order_id aside. Mechanically these look exactly like the duplicate order rows in the worked example above. But they are not duplicates at all, they are two real, separate purchases. Removing one of them would understate that customer's actual spending and quietly corrupt any analysis built on top of the transaction table.

blocks.title: Domain awareness beats a mechanical rule
blocks.content: Before removing anything, ask whether the entity you are deduplicating (a customer, a form submission, a sensor reading) is the kind of thing that can legitimately repeat. Customer signups should not repeat. Purchases, sensor readings, and log events often can, and sometimes should.

blocks.text: 9. Common Mistakes

items: Checking for duplicates before normalizing text case and whitespace, which lets a huge share of real duplicates hide in plain sight because 'Ravi' and 'ravi ' are technically different strings.
Only ever checking for exact duplicates and assuming that is the whole problem, missing the near duplicates entirely because nobody looked for them.
Running drop_duplicates() on the entire row by default when a subset of key columns, like email or customer ID, would have been the correct and safer definition of what counts as the same record.

blocks.text: 10. Recap And Checklist
When you hit a new duplicates problem, work through it in this order.

items: Run df.duplicated().sum() first to see how big the problem is before deciding anything.
Decide what actually defines uniqueness for this dataset: the whole row, or a subset like email or customer ID.
Normalize text, case and whitespace, before checking for duplicates, not after.
Pick keep='first', keep='last', or keep=False deliberately, based on which copy is actually more trustworthy, not by default.
Ask whether this entity can legitimately repeat in the real world before removing anything, especially for transaction or event style data.
For near duplicates, treat a similarity score as a shortlist for review, not an automatic deletion trigger.
